newsitem.title: CHINA: Hopewell says weaker baht inflates costs.
newsitem.headline: Hopewell says weaker baht inflates costs.

text.p: Hopewell Holdings Ltd chairman Gordon Wu said on Monday the de facto devaluation of the Thai baht had increased the cost of the company's Bangkok mass transit railway project by 15 percent.
Wu said the higher cost meant the railway project would need to charge a slightly higher fare to passengers.
"Once we have that agreement in, I believe, about three months' time then we can have an amended agreement and then we can proceed forward," he told reporters.
Wu said the financing structure for the project was unchanged and in place, and that the financiers were ready to lend the necessary money.
"The financing structure is in place, the export credit people and the commercial bank people are ready to go but I am not ready to take the money because I want to make sure I can repay," Wu said.
"I don't want to proceed until I get a fare rise."

Hopewell said on Friday it was unable to complete its long-delayed Bangkok Elevated Rail Train System (BERTS) as planned due to the decline in Thailand's economy and the de facto devaluation of the baht.
In the company's preliminary contact with the Thai government, both sides were sincere in their desire to proceed with the project, Wu said on Monday.
There was no chance of writing off the project and Hopewell was under no cash pressure, he added.
Wu dismissed rumours Hopewell shares would be sold to raise cash.
Hopewell has been wrangling with successive Thai governments for a decade over the US$3.2 billion elevated road and rail transit scheme which was slated to be finished by 1999.
The first phase was due to be completed by next year.
The Thai government has threatened to fine the company 7.5 million baht for each day of delay in the first phase, up to a maximum of 134 days.
The company on Friday estimated that around 30 percent of the 40-km first phase had been completed, and that it had spent about US$560 million on the project.

Hopewell (Thailand) Ltd said the baht's fall would raise the project's original 80 billion baht investment by at least 10 billion and that prospective bank creditors would not support the project until a new feasibility study was done.
Wu said on Monday the baht's decline raised costs because much of the equipment was priced in U.S. dollars.

Aside from currency problems, the project had been delayed by difficulties acquiring land, he said. In one case, workers sent to a site central to the project were arrested for trespassing on private property, he said.
